0.title: Something Wrong with Me
0.essay:
You may never have used the word. But you know the feeling. An old memory surfaces and your face burns. Someone looks at you a little too closely and you want to disappear. Under everything lies a quiet belief: if people really knew me, they would turn away. Not “I did something wrong”, but “I am something wrong”. That is shame, and this study is for you.

An old wound with a name

Shame appears in the Bible’s third chapter, and the words shame, disgrace and reproach run through the Psalms and the prophets. Some of it is shame we brought on ourselves. Much of it was put on people by others: by cruelty, rejection, poverty or illness. Scripture is honest about both kinds, and it does not leave either where it found it.

The promise of the Bible is not that shame will be explained away, but that it will be lifted. “Those who look to him are radiant, and their faces shall never be ashamed” (Psalm 34:5). That is a promise about faces, the very part of us that shame wants to hide.

Where we are going

We will name shame in plain words and see how it behaves. We will go back to the garden, where shame began and where God first covered it. We will look at the two roots of shame, what we have done and what was done to us, and ask how healthy shame differs from the kind that only crushes. We will watch Jesus meet ashamed people face to face. We will stand at the cross, where he bore our shame and clothed us with himself. And we will end with practical wisdom for living in the light.

This study builds on the short section on guilt and shame in The Truth About Sin. If your struggle is mainly about not forgiving yourself, see Perfectionism & Self-Condemnation; if it is a decision you cannot undo, see Regret & the Past.

The chapters

“I Am Wrong”: Naming Shame; Naked and Hiding; “Where Could I Carry My Shame?”; “Daughter”: Jesus and the Ashamed; Despising the Shame; and Into the Light.

For reflection

When did you last feel the urge to hide, not because of something you did, but because of who you felt you were? What would it mean for you to lift your face?

1.title: “I Am Wrong”: Naming Shame
1.essay:
Guilt and shame often arrive together, and we use the words loosely. But they are not the same. Learning to tell them apart is one of the first kindnesses we can do ourselves, because each needs a different word from God.

Two voices

Guilt says, “I did wrong.” Shame says, “I am wrong.” Guilt points at a deed: a lie told, a promise broken. Shame points at the self: I am dirty, I am too much, I am not enough, I do not belong. Guilt can be confessed and forgiven, and then it is finished. Shame feels as if there is nothing to confess, only something to hide, because the problem seems to be me.

Guilt is first a fact before God, whether we feel it or not. Shame is about how we stand before eyes: God’s eyes, other people’s, and our own. It is the sense of being seen and found unworthy. That is why it burns in the face. We blush, look down, turn away.

Four faces of shame

Shame shows itself in at least four ways, and most of us know one or two of them well.

Exposure. The feeling of being naked in front of others, seen in our weakness or failure when we wanted to be covered. A mistake in front of a room, a secret that comes out, a body we wish no one could see.

Unworthiness. The sense of being less than others, not good enough to be loved or wanted. When Peter saw Jesus’ power, he fell down and said, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” (Luke 5:8). He felt too small and too stained to be near him.

Defilement. The feeling of being dirty, stained in a way washing cannot reach. Isaiah, seeing the Lord, cried, “Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). Those who have been abused often feel this most of all, though the stain belongs to the one who harmed them.

Not belonging. The sense of being on the outside, unwanted, a burden. Under the law of Moses a person with a serious skin disease had to “cry out, ‘Unclean, unclean’” and “live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp” (Leviticus 13:45–46). Many people today live outside the camp in their own minds, even when sitting in a full church.

How shame behaves

Shame has habits. It hides: it keeps secrets, avoids eyes, leaves early. It covers: it builds a better image, through achievement, humour, a perfect home or a busy ministry. It numbs: through food, screens, drink, or simply never being still. It attacks: some people, when they feel small, become sharp and blaming, because it is easier to point at others than to be looked at. And it silences. Shame rarely speaks its own name. It simply makes us quieter, more careful, more alone.

Notice that none of these habits brings healing. Each one keeps the wound hidden, and wounds that are hidden do not heal.

Shame is about people, too

In much of the world, and in the world of the Bible, honour and shame are the main way people think about right and wrong. A family’s name matters more than an individual’s feelings, and to be disgraced is to be cut off. Western people often think of themselves as guilt-based rather than shame-based, but shame is everywhere: in social media, in schools, in the fear of being cancelled, in the quiet judgments about weight, money and success. The gospel speaks to both. Christ answers our guilt before God’s law and our shame before every watching eye.

An example

A woman in her forties has attended the same church for years. She sits near the back and slips out during the last hymn. People think she is shy. In fact, ever since her marriage ended, she has felt marked, as if everyone can see that she is the one who failed. She has confessed her own part in it many times and believes she is forgiven. What she has never done is let anyone close enough to see her. Guilt has been dealt with; shame has not.

Naming it is the beginning

To call shame by its name is not to wallow in it. It is to bring it out where God can speak to it. The rest of this study is about what he says. And the first thing he says is that shame is not part of what he made us to be.

For reflection

Can you think of a time when you felt shame rather than guilt? Which of the four faces, exposure, unworthiness, defilement or not belonging, do you know best? Which of shame’s habits do you recognise in yourself: hiding, covering, numbing, attacking or going silent? Is there anything you have confessed to God but never let anyone else see?

2.title: Naked and Hiding
2.essay:
The Bible’s story of shame begins with two people who had none. Then something happened, and they reached for leaves. Genesis 2 and 3 tell us where shame came from, what we still do with it, and, most wonderfully, what God did about it.

Naked and not ashamed

The account of creation ends with a quiet sentence: “And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed” (Genesis 2:25). They were completely seen and completely at ease. There was nothing to hide, from each other or from God. To be fully known and fully loved was simply normal. This is what we were made for, and it is why shame always feels like something gone wrong. It is.

Eyes opened

The serpent promised that if they ate, their eyes would be opened. They were. “Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked. And they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths” (Genesis 3:7). Their bodies had not changed. What had changed was everything around them. Having turned from God, they could no longer bear to be seen. Being looked at now felt dangerous.

Notice the fig leaves. This is the first human attempt to deal with shame, and it is a cover. We have been sewing fig leaves ever since. Ours are made of achievement, image, cleverness, busyness, even religion. They are better than nothing, and they never quite work. Leaves wither.

Hiding from the one who could help

Then came the sound of God in the garden, “and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden” (Genesis 3:8). Shame always turns us away from the very person who could heal it. Adam explained, “I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself” (Genesis 3:10). Shame and fear go together. When we feel exposed, we run.

Within moments came blame. “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate” (Genesis 3:12). The woman blamed the serpent. Shame breaks relationships: first with God, then with each other, then with the world.

“Who told you?”

God answered Adam with a question: “Who told you that you were naked?” (Genesis 3:11). It is worth asking of our own shame. Shame has a voice. Sometimes that voice is our conscience telling the truth about something we have done. But often it is another voice: a parent who mocked us, a bully at school, an abuser, a culture that measures worth by beauty or money, or the Accuser himself. Before we believe what shame says, we should ask where it learned to speak.

God makes clothes

The chapter that tells of the fall also tells of judgment: pain, toil, death, and exile from the garden. But before the man and woman leave, there is a sentence of astonishing tenderness: “And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them” (Genesis 3:21).

The fig leaves were their covering. The skins were his. They were better, warmer and more lasting, and God himself put them on. The holy God, whom they had just disobeyed, did not leave them naked. He covered their shame with his own hands.

The text does not tell us why skins, or what it meant that an animal died. Many Christians have seen here a first hint of something the rest of the Bible makes plain: that our covering comes at a cost, and that God himself would one day pay it. We should hold that hint lightly, but it is not fanciful. From this point the theme of clothing runs through Scripture. God tells Israel, in a picture of covenant love, “I spread the corner of my garment over you and covered your nakedness” (Ezekiel 16:8). The risen Christ offers “white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be seen” (Revelation 3:18). The story that began with nakedness ends with a wedding robe.

Love covers

A few chapters later, Noah lay drunk and uncovered in his tent. One son, Ham, saw and told others. The other two “took a garment, laid it on both their shoulders, and walked backward and covered the nakedness of their father” (Genesis 9:23). Here is love that covers another’s shame instead of spreading it. “Love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). That does not mean hiding crimes or protecting abusers, which Scripture never allows. It means refusing to make a spectacle of other people’s weakness.

An example

A man in his thirties is the life of every gathering. He is quick with a joke, especially at his own expense. Only his wife knows how tired he is, and how frightened that if he stopped performing, people would see the anxious, ordinary man underneath. Reading Genesis 3 in a home group, he realises that his humour is a fig leaf. It is not wicked. But it is not working, and he is weary of sewing.

For reflection

What fig leaves do you tend to reach for? When shame speaks to you, whose voice does it sound like? What does Genesis 3:21 tell you about God’s heart towards people who have just failed? Is there someone whose weakness you could cover in love, rather than expose?

3.title: “Where Could I Carry My Shame?”
3.essay:
Not all shame is the same. Some of it rises from what we have done. Some of it was put on us by what others did, or by what happened to us. Often the two are tangled together. It matters to tell them apart, because the remedy is not identical.

Shame from our own sin

When we sin, it is right to feel something. Ezra, grieving over the sins of his people, prayed, “O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God, for our iniquities have risen higher than our heads” (Ezra 9:6). Paul asked the Roman Christians, “what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans 6:21). In these places shame is simply honesty. It sees sin as it is.

Indeed, Scripture treats the inability to feel shame as a danger sign. Of a hardened people God said, “they were not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush” (Jeremiah 6:15). A conscience that can still blush is a gift.

Healthy and unhealthy shame

So how do we tell shame that helps from shame that only harms? Paul gives a clue: “For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). Healthy shame is specific: it points at something real that was wrong. It turns us towards God, like the prodigal heading home. And it ends: when the sin is confessed and forgiven, it has done its work, and we are free to lift our heads. Unhealthy shame is vague and global: not “I did that” but “I am rubbish”. It drives us away from God and others. And it never ends, no matter how often we confess. It also attaches itself to things that are not sin at all: a body, a disability, poverty, a family background, or having been a victim.

Christians differ in how they speak about this. Some say shame is always destructive and should simply be rejected: God wants us free of it. Others say shame is a moral emotion that God built into us, and that a culture which tries to abolish it loses the ability to repent. Both are guarding something true.

This commentary’s view: shame over real sin is right and healthy when it leads us to Christ, and it is meant to end there. Once sin is confessed and forgiven, the believer is not summoned to go on wearing it; to do so treats Christ’s covering as too thin. Shame that is not about sin at all, or that will not let go after forgiveness, is not God’s voice and should be answered with his word.

Shame put on us

Tamar was a king’s daughter. Her half-brother Amnon tricked her into his room. She pleaded with him, and then asked a question that every victim of abuse will understand: “As for me, where could I carry my shame?” (2 Samuel 13:13). She knew the shame would fall on her, though the sin would be his. He raped her, then threw her out and bolted the door.

She was wearing “a long robe with sleeves, for thus were the virgin daughters of the king dressed” (2 Samuel 13:18). It was the sign of her honour. “And Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long robe that she wore” (2 Samuel 13:19). Her brother Absalom told her, “hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother; do not take this to heart” (2 Samuel 13:20). Silence, on top of the wrong. “So Tamar lived, a desolate woman, in her brother Absalom’s house” (2 Samuel 13:20).

Notice how Scripture tells this story. It does not hide it. It calls the deed Amnon’s “outrageous thing” (2 Samuel 13:12), not hers. It keeps her name. The shame Tamar felt was real, but it belonged to her abuser. That is true for every person who has been abused: what was done to you defiled the one who did it, not you.

Others carry shame for things that were never sin. Hannah could not have children, “her rival used to provoke her grievously” (1 Samuel 1:6), year after year. When the priest wrongly thought her drunk, she begged, “Do not regard your servant as a worthless woman” (1 Samuel 1:16). People carry shame for being poor, for being ill, for being disabled, for being rejected by a parent, for the colour of their skin or the accent of their voice. To all of them God says, “For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in” (Psalm 27:10).

Safety first

If you are being harmed now, or a child is, safety comes first. Tell someone you trust, and contact the police or the authorities whose job it is to protect. Abuse is a crime, and churches must report it, never handle it quietly. If you are carrying the shame of past abuse, please seek help from a counsellor who understands trauma, alongside your church. This is not a lack of faith. The study Biblical Counseling has a chapter on trauma and abuse for those who care for survivors.

An example

A man in his fifties has never told anyone that a coach abused him as a boy. He has always felt dirty and somehow responsible. One evening he tells his pastor. The pastor’s first words are, “That was not your fault, and I am so sorry.” Together they contact the police, and the pastor helps him find a counsellor. It is the start of a long road. But for the first time, the shame has somewhere to go.

For reflection

Is the shame you carry mainly from what you have done, from what was done to you, or both? Does your shame look more like the healthy kind or the unhealthy kind described here? Who in your life has said to you, in effect, “hold your peace”, and who has stood with you? If you were abused, have you been able to tell anyone safe?

4.title: “Daughter”: Jesus and the Ashamed
4.essay:
If you want to know how God treats ashamed people, watch Jesus. Again and again in the Gospels he goes towards those whom everyone else avoided. He looks at them, speaks to them, touches them, and sends them back into the world with their heads up.

A woman who came from behind

Mark tells of “a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse” (Mark 5:25–26). Under the law her condition made her ritually unclean, “all the days of the discharge” (Leviticus 15:25), and anyone she touched became unclean too. For twelve years she had been ill, poor, untouchable and, in a sense, outside.

So she did not come to Jesus openly. She “came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment” (Mark 5:27). That is what shame does: it approaches from behind, hoping not to be noticed. And she was healed at once.

But Jesus would not let her slip away. He turned and asked, “Who touched my garments?” (Mark 5:30). It can seem harsh, but it was mercy. A secret healing would have mended her body and left her shame untouched. So she “came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth” (Mark 5:33). Everyone heard. And Jesus said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease” (Mark 5:34). The woman who had crept up from behind, unclean and alone, was publicly named as family.

Notice something else. By the law, her touch should have made Jesus unclean. Instead, his cleanness flowed into her. It was the same with the leper whom Jesus “stretched out his hand and touched” (Mark 1:41). With Jesus, holiness is contagious, and shame is what gets washed away.

A woman at a well

In John 4 Jesus sits by a well “about the sixth hour” (John 4:6), around noon, in the heat. A Samaritan woman comes to draw water. Some think she came at that hour to avoid the other women; the text does not say, and we cannot be sure. But she was a Samaritan, whom Jews avoided, and a woman, whom rabbis did not speak with in public, and her life was complicated. Jesus said, “Go, call your husband, and come here” (John 4:16). She answered, “I have no husband.” He said, “you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband” (John 4:18).

We are not told why she had had five husbands. In that world a woman could be widowed or divorced through no fault of her own. But her situation was irregular, and Jesus named it. Here is the wonder: he named it without rejecting her. He went on talking with her, and to her, more plainly than to almost anyone, he said who he was: “I who speak to you am he” (John 4:26).

She left her water jar and ran into the town: “Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did” (John 4:29). The thing she had probably avoided people over became the first words of her witness. To be fully known and not turned away: that is the end of shame.

A man up a tree

Zacchaeus was “a chief tax collector and was rich” (Luke 19:2). Tax collectors worked for the Roman occupiers and often grew rich by overcharging their own people. He had earned his bad name. He was also small, and he climbed a tree to see Jesus. Jesus stopped beneath it and called him by name: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today” (Luke 19:5).

To be a guest in someone’s house was to honour them in public. The crowd knew it: “they all grumbled, ‘He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner’” (Luke 19:7). Jesus took on Zacchaeus’s disgrace by being seen with him. And notice the order. The welcome came first; the change followed. Zacchaeus stood and promised to give half his goods to the poor and to repay fourfold anyone he had cheated (Luke 19:8). Jesus declared, “Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham” (Luke 19:9). The man who had been cast out was named as belonging.

The pattern

Jesus’ enemies summed up his ministry in one complaint: “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (Luke 15:2). They meant it as an insult. It is the best news an ashamed person could hear. He sees us when we come from behind. He names what is hidden, not to humiliate us but to free us. He touches what others avoid. And he calls us family.

An example

A man comes out of prison and starts attending a church near his hostel. He sits alone, sure that everyone knows. After a few weeks one of the elders and his wife invite him home for Sunday lunch. Later the man says it was the first time in years that someone had not been afraid to be seen with him. He did not need a lecture. He needed a table.

For reflection

Which of these three people is most like you, and why? Why do you think Jesus made the healed woman come forward? What does it mean to you that the woman at the well was fully known and not rejected? Who might be sitting alone near you, waiting for someone to be seen with them?

5.title: Despising the Shame
5.essay:
Every story of shame in Scripture leads to one place: a hill outside Jerusalem. There the Son of God was stripped, mocked and hung up before the world. He did not only bear our guilt there. He bore our shame, so that we could be clothed, honoured and welcomed.

A death designed to shame

Crucifixion was not only painful. It was built to humiliate. The victim was stripped and displayed in public, beside a road, so that everyone could see his helplessness. Before Jesus was crucified, the soldiers “stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him” (Matthew 27:28) and knelt in mockery, and “they spit on him” (Matthew 27:30). At the cross they divided his clothes, fulfilling the psalm: “They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots” (John 19:24). Isaiah had foreseen it: “I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6).

Think of who this was. The eternal Son, through whom all things were made, was the Lord who clothed Adam and Eve in the garden. Now he hung without his own clothes. He was “despised and rejected by men … and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised” (Isaiah 53:3). Every face of shame met in him.

Outside the camp

The letter to the Hebrews notes where it happened. The bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp. “So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). Outside the camp was where the unclean lived, where the leper cried out his warning, where the rejected were sent. Jesus went to the place of the outsider. He took the outside place so that outsiders could be brought in.

Despising the shame

Hebrews tells us to look “to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God” (Hebrews 12:2). He felt the shame fully. To despise it means he did not let it have the last word or turn him back. He counted it as nothing beside the joy ahead. And what was that joy? It included us: “bringing many sons to glory” (Hebrews 2:10). He walked through the shame because he wanted his people with him.

Here is the exchange at the heart of the gospel. “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). He took our sin and our shame; we receive his righteousness and his honour. The shame that should have been ours was carried outside the camp and left there.

Clothed

So the Bible speaks of believers as clothed. “I will greatly rejoice in the LORD; my soul shall exult in my God, for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness” (Isaiah 61:10). Zechariah saw the high priest Joshua in filthy garments, and heard the Lord say, “Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments” (Zechariah 3:4). Paul writes, “For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27). Baptism, given to those who believe, is the outward sign of what faith has already received: we are wrapped in Christ himself. When God looks at a believer, he sees his Son.

Jesus painted the same picture in a story. A younger son came home in disgrace, rehearsing his speech: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke 15:21). But the father had already run to him, and now he did not let him finish. “Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet” (Luke 15:22). The robe covered the rags. The ring spoke of belonging. Shoes were for sons, not servants. It is often pointed out that in that culture a dignified older man did not run. This father did, taking the indignity on himself so that his son would be covered before the village could see him.

Honoured

Mephibosheth was Jonathan’s son and King Saul’s grandson. He was dropped as a child of five and was lame from then on (2 Samuel 4:4). When David became king, Mephibosheth was living quietly at Lo-debar. He was the grandson of a fallen king. David sent for him. Mephibosheth fell on his face and said, “What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?” (2 Samuel 9:8). But David said, “Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan … and you shall eat at my table always” (2 Samuel 9:7).

So Mephibosheth “ate at David’s table, like one of the king’s sons” (2 Samuel 9:11). The chapter ends, “Now he was lame in both his feet” (2 Samuel 9:13). He was still lame. Nothing in him had earned the seat. He was there for another’s sake. So are we, for Jesus’ sake. Our weaknesses do not disqualify us from the King’s table, and his welcome does not wait for them to vanish.

Not ashamed

The most astonishing words on this subject are about God himself. Of his people Jesus “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11). And of those who look for his city, “God is not ashamed to be called their God” (Hebrews 11:16). The one whose opinion matters most has looked at you, with everything you have done and everything done to you, and is not ashamed to be seen with you. So “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame” (Romans 10:11). And God promises, “I will change their shame into praise and renown in all the earth” (Zephaniah 3:19).

An example

A woman who became a Christian in her thirties has never felt she quite belongs among people who grew up in church. At the Lord’s Supper one Sunday the minister reads Hebrews 2:11. She finds herself weeping. Jesus is not embarrassed by her. For the first time she lifts her head as she takes the bread.

For reflection

What moves you most about the shame Jesus bore at the cross? What does it mean for you to be “clothed” with Christ? Where do you see yourself in the story of Mephibosheth? Read Hebrews 2:11 slowly. What changes if Jesus is not ashamed of you?

6.title: Into the Light
6.essay:
Shame grows in the dark and weakens in the light. The gospel does not only tell us that Christ has covered our shame; it calls us out of hiding to live as people who are clothed. Here is some practical wisdom for that, offered not as a new performance but as a way of walking in what Christ has done.

Bring the hidden thing into the light

Jesus said that “everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed” (John 3:20). Shame keeps us in the shadows even when we have nothing left to hide. But “if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7). David knew what silence cost him: “For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away” (Psalm 32:3). Relief came when he “did not cover” his iniquity (Psalm 32:5).

Coming into the light usually means telling someone. “Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16). And if your shame comes from what was done to you, telling someone is not confession at all; it is letting someone help carry what was never yours.

Choose safe people

Not everyone is safe, and not everyone needs to know everything. Choose someone who is mature, kind, trustworthy and discreet. “Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered” (Proverbs 11:13). It may be a pastor, an older Christian, a close friend or a trained counsellor. Start small. Watch how they handle a little before you trust them with more. If what you share involves abuse or danger to anyone, a safe person will help you get proper help, and will not keep a crime secret.

Answer shame’s lies

Shame speaks in lies that sound like facts. It helps to name them and answer them with God’s word, out loud if need be. Remember God’s question in the garden: “Who told you that you were naked?” (Genesis 3:11).

“You are what you did.” But Paul, after listing grievous sins, says, “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 6:11). “You are what was done to you.” But what was done to you defiled the one who did it, and you are “a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). “If they really knew you, they would leave.” But Jesus already knows, and says, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). “God is disgusted with you.” But “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

Feelings follow truth slowly. Keep speaking it. In time the old voice grows quieter.

In the moment

Shame often floods in suddenly: a memory, a mistake in front of others, a look from someone. Your face burns and everything in you wants to hide or hit back. Breathe. Pray a few words: “O my God, in you I trust; let me not be put to shame” (Psalm 25:2). Remember that you are clothed. Then take one small honest step: stay in the room, finish the sentence, admit the mistake without collapsing. If you did something wrong, confess it and put it right. Healthy shame should be dealt with quickly and then laid down, not carried for years.

The church as a place of welcome

A church should be the safest room in town for ashamed people. “Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God” (Romans 15:7). Paul says that in the body of Christ, “on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor” (1 Corinthians 12:23). The church gives most honour to those the world overlooks.

That means no gossip. It means sitting with the person who sits alone. It means being as glad to see the divorced, the poor, the ill, the disabled and the ex-offender as anyone else. It means stories of grace told honestly from the front, so that no one thinks they are the only failure in the room. And it means never shaming victims or shielding abusers. At the Lord’s Table, every one of us eats like Mephibosheth: there for another’s sake.

When you need more help

Deep shame can be tied up with depression, trauma, eating disorders or self-harm. Seeing a doctor or a qualified counsellor is not a failure of faith; God often gives help through such means, and medicine is a good gift. The studies Depression & the Christian and Biblical Counseling say more.

If shame ever leads to thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, please get help now. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust. Your life is precious to God.

An example

A student has hidden an eating disorder from everyone for two years. One night she texts an older woman from church: “Can we talk? It’s hard to say.” Over coffee she says it. The older woman does not look shocked. She listens, prays, and the next week goes with her to the doctor. Months later the student says the hardest moment was pressing send, and the best was seeing that her friend’s face did not change.

Further reading

Edward T. Welch’s Shame Interrupted is a warm, Bible-saturated book on this subject. Curt Thompson’s The Soul of Shame, by a Christian psychiatrist, explores how shame works in our minds and relationships.

One day shame will be gone for good. God promises, “you will forget the shame of your youth” (Isaiah 54:4), and the one on the throne says, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5). Until then, every step into the light is a step towards that day.

For reflection

Is there something you have kept hidden that you need to bring into the light, and who would be a safe person to tell? Which of shame’s lies do you hear most often, and which verse answers it? What one small step could you take the next time shame floods in? How could you help your church be a place where ashamed people are welcomed?
